inResponse.head: No thesis or named business
inResponse.quote: Marketing is very important for every business
inResponse.why: This sentence makes a general statement that could appear in any response. The question asks you to evaluate strategies for a specific business you studied, so the opening must name that business, state its {{marketing objectives|the specific goals a business sets for its marketing activities, such as increasing market share or building brand awareness|0}}, and give your overall judgement on whether the strategies achieved them.

inResponse.head: Business unnamed, no evidence
inResponse.quote: A business I studied used advertising and social media to sell its products and it worked well
inResponse.why: The business is never identified, which means no case study evidence can be accepted by a marker. You must name the business, specify the strategies used, and explain what outcome shows they worked, rather than simply stating 'it worked well'.

inResponse.head: Assertion restates P1 with no analysis
inResponse.quote: Marketing strategies help businesses to make more money, so they are effective
inResponse.why: This sentence repeats the general claim that strategies are effective without explaining which strategy, how it served which {{marketing objective|the specific, measurable goals that guide a business's marketing activities|0}}, and what evidence shows the result. Every body paragraph needs a point, an explanation of the mechanism, and specific evidence.

inResponse.head: No weighing of effectiveness
inResponse.why: An 'evaluate' question requires you to weigh how effective the strategies were, which means acknowledging any limitations or areas where the strategies fell short, as well as their strengths. Without this, the response only presents one side and cannot reach the higher bands.

inResponse.head: No conclusion
inResponse.why: The response ends without a conclusion. A conclusion must bring together the overall judgement on how effectively the strategies achieved the business's marketing objectives, referring back to the objectives named in the introduction.

inResponse.head: No objectives stated
inResponse.quote: Its target market is teenagers aged 13 to 17, and its marketing strategies cover the four Ps of the marketing mix
inResponse.why: The question asks you to evaluate strategies against {{marketing objectives|the specific goals a business sets for its marketing activity, such as increasing market share, building brand awareness or growing customer loyalty|0}}. Without naming at least two objectives here, every paragraph that follows can only describe what Northline does, never judge whether it works. Replace the four-Ps frame with a sentence that states what Northline is actually trying to achieve.

inResponse.head: Missing evaluative thesis
inResponse.why: An evaluate question requires you to state your overall verdict in the introduction. Without a thesis, the marker has no argument to follow across the paragraphs. Add one sentence that gives your overall judgement on whether the strategies are effective, partially effective, or mixed.

inResponse.head: Description, not evaluation
inResponse.quote: For product, Northline sells running shoes, training gear and a range of hoodies
inResponse.why: Listing what Northline sells is description, not analysis. You need to explain how this product range serves a specific {{marketing objective|the specific goal a business sets for its marketing activity|0}}, such as why stocking these three categories positions Northline to attract its teenage target market rather than a broader audience.

inResponse.head: Assertion without evidence
inResponse.quote: It releases new designs each season and uses bright colours that appeal to its target market
inResponse.why: Saying bright colours 'appeal to its target market' is an assertion: no evidence is given for why teenagers respond to this or whether it has actually increased sales or awareness. You need to link the seasonal release cycle or the colour choices to a measurable outcome or at least explain the mechanism by which this achieves the objective.

inResponse.head: Strategy change not evaluated
inResponse.quote: For promotion, Northline moved from print advertising to short videos on social media platforms
inResponse.why: Moving from print to social media video is the most strategically significant fact in the response, yet you do not say why this change was made, what objective it serves, or whether it worked. Explain the reasoning: teenagers consume content on social media rather than print, so this shift directly targets the awareness objective for that segment.

inResponse.head: Influencer use not evaluated
inResponse.quote: The videos show young athletes wearing its products, and some of them feature influencers
inResponse.why: You mention {{influencer marketing|using individuals with a social media following to promote products to their audience|0}} but do not explain why it is effective for Northline's objectives or provide any measure of its impact, such as follower reach, engagement or brand sentiment change. Add a reason why this technique works for the teenage target market.

inResponse.head: Loyalty strategy not linked to objective
inResponse.quote: It also has a loyalty app where members get early access to new releases
inResponse.why: Early access through a loyalty app is a classic {{customer retention|strategies aimed at keeping existing customers buying from the business rather than switching to competitors|0}} tool, but you do not connect it to any objective such as building customer loyalty or repeat purchase rates. Without that link, the sentence is a description of a feature, not an evaluation of a strategy.

inResponse.head: Distribution not linked to objectives
inResponse.quote: For place, Northline sells through its own stores in shopping centres and through its website, which offers free delivery on orders over $80
inResponse.why: You describe two channels but do not explain why having both a physical presence and an online store helps Northline reach its teenage target market or achieve its objectives. The $80 free-delivery threshold is a specific business decision that deserves an explanation of what it is meant to do, such as raising average order value or encouraging first-time online buyers.

inResponse.head: Price change not explained or evaluated
inResponse.quote: For price, Northline reduced its prices across the range in 2023
inResponse.why: A bare statement that prices were reduced in 2023 does not show any understanding of {{pricing strategy|the method a business uses to set prices in order to achieve its marketing objectives|0}}. You need to explain why the reduction was made, which objective it serves, and whether there is any evidence it worked, such as a sales volume increase or a change in market share.

inResponse.head: Conclusion is a restatement, not a judgement
inResponse.quote: These are the main marketing strategies that Northline uses, and they help it to achieve its marketing objectives
inResponse.why: An evaluate question requires a conclusion that weighs the evidence and delivers a final verdict. Saying 'they help it to achieve its marketing objectives' simply repeats the topic without distinguishing which strategies were most effective, which were less effective, and why. This sentence earns no marks because it adds no reasoning that was not already present.

inResponse.head: Name the strategy type
inResponse.quote: The move from print to short-form video was effective against that objective
inResponse.why: The phrase 'move from print to short-form video' describes what the business did but does not place it inside the course's framework. Naming it as a shift in the {{promotional mix|the combination of promotional methods a business uses to communicate with its target market|0}} would satisfy the knowledge and terminology criteria and signal that the choice was strategic rather than incidental.

inResponse.head: Connect reach to market share
inResponse.why: The paragraph shows the strategy was cheap and reached the right people, but it does not explicitly connect increased reach to movement in {{market share|the proportion of total sales in a market held by one business|0}}. Without that step, the reader must make the inference themselves, which limits the mark under 'sustained, logical and cohesive response'.

inResponse.head: Name the relationship strategy
inResponse.quote: The loyalty app was also effective, because members bought 2.4 times a year against 1.3 for non-members, which turned reach into repeat purchase
inResponse.why: The loyalty app is an instrument of {{relationship marketing|strategies that focus on building long-term connections with customers to increase retention and lifetime value|0}}, and naming it as such would show that the student understands why the strategy was chosen, not just what it did. Replacing 'loyalty app' with its conceptual category earns a mark under both knowledge and terminology.

inResponse.head: Name the pricing strategy and its effect on positioning
inResponse.quote: Northline cut prices across its range in the same year, and its average sale value fell 11 per cent, which undermined the premium image the video campaign was building
inResponse.why: The student shows the 11 per cent fall in average sale value but does not name this as a {{penetration pricing|setting a low price to attract customers and grow market share, often at the cost of margin and brand perception|0}} or price-reduction strategy, nor does it connect it to the concept of {{brand positioning|the place a brand occupies in the consumer's mind relative to competitors|0}}. Naming both terms would lift this paragraph from observation into analysis.

inResponse.head: Commit to the final judgement
inResponse.quote: Overall the strategies were largely effective: share reached 11 per cent, close to the target, but the pricing decision cost margin and probably limited how much of the gain will last
inResponse.why: The student wrote 'probably limited how much of the gain will last', but paragraph four already established that the pricing decision undermined the premium image and cost margin. The evidence supports a firm claim, so 'probably' weakens a conclusion the argument has already earned. Removing the hedge and tying the judgement to the original benchmark (12 per cent vs 11 per cent) would close the response at the same evaluative level at which it opened.

inResponse.head: Thesis gives no verdict

inResponse.head: Causal link is asserted, not shown

inResponse.why: The sentence tells the reader that the app increases {{customer lifetime value|the total revenue a business expects from a single customer over the entire relationship|0}}, but gives no figure, trend, or specific feature of the app that produced that outcome. inResponse.head: Opening claim is too general

inResponse.why: This sentence restates a principle without connecting it to Northline's specific pricing decision or objective. A marker rewarding evaluation wants to see the principle applied immediately to the case.

inResponse.head: Evidence is a single throwaway clause

inResponse.why: 'Which happened at Northline' is the only business-specific detail in this paragraph, but it carries no explanation of what the discounting was, when it occurred, or how it damaged the premium position. inResponse.head: No tie-back to the objective

inResponse.why: A conclusion to an evaluate question must deliver a clear, supported judgement: the strategies were effective, partially effective, or ineffective, and why. inResponse.head: Missing thesis judgement
inResponse.quote: Northline Sportswear's marketing objective in 2023 was to increase its share of the 13 to 17 year old market from 8 to 12 per cent
inResponse.why: The objective is stated but the response does not signal how effective the strategies were overall. A Band 5 or 6 response opens with a controlling judgement that the body then proves.

inResponse.head: Wrong term: price skimming
inResponse.quote: Its most effective strategy was price skimming
inResponse.why: {{price skimming|a strategy of setting a high launch price and lowering it over time to capture different consumer segments|0}} means charging a premium price first, not reducing prices broadly. The strategy Northline appears to have used is {{penetration pricing|setting a low price to attract a large number of buyers and gain market share quickly|0}} or a price reduction strategy. Using the wrong term here loses all the marks for this strategy.

inResponse.head: Unsupported absolute claim
inResponse.quote: Northline lowered its prices across its whole range, which is called price skimming, and because teenagers have limited money, lowering prices always increases sales
inResponse.why: The statement that lowering prices always increases sales ignores {{price elasticity of demand|the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price|0}}. Whether a price cut lifts sales depends on how elastic demand is in the segment. Replacing 'always' with a qualified, evidence-linked claim is necessary for any marks here.

inResponse.head: Incorrect profit reasoning
inResponse.quote: When sales increase, profit always increases too, so the price cut also improved Northline's profitability
inResponse.why: Higher sales volume does not automatically mean higher profit. If {{contribution margin|the selling price minus variable cost per unit|0}} falls with the price cut, total profit may decline even as units sold rise. The student's own evidence, the 11 per cent drop in average sale value, makes this concern concrete but is then ignored.

inResponse.head: Evidence dismissed without evaluation
inResponse.quote: Even though the average sale value fell by 11 per cent, this does not matter because more customers were buying
inResponse.why: Dismissing the 11 per cent fall as irrelevant removes the only piece of quantitative evidence in the paragraph. Evaluation means weighing evidence, not setting it aside. This sentence loses the chance to demonstrate evaluative thinking, which is what the question asks for.

inResponse.head: Mass marketing confused with segmented targeting
inResponse.quote: Social media is a form of mass marketing because everyone uses it, so Northline reached the whole market rather than one segment, which is the best way to gain market share
inResponse.why: {{Mass marketing|a strategy of offering one product to the entire market without segmentation|0}} means ignoring segment differences and appealing to everyone with a single message. Social media platforms such as TikTok or Instagram allow precise {{market segmentation|dividing a market into groups with shared characteristics to target them separately|0}} by age, interest and behaviour. Northline was specifically targeting the 13 to 17 year old segment, which is the opposite of mass marketing.

inResponse.head: Incorrect claim about market share growth
inResponse.quote: The loyalty app was the least effective strategy, because giving members early access to new products is a cost to the business and does not attract new customers, and market share only grows from new customers
inResponse.why: {{Market share|a business's sales as a proportion of total industry sales|0}} can grow through new customer acquisition, but also through increased purchase frequency or spend from existing customers, or through competitor decline. A loyalty app that retains high-spending existing customers can contribute to market share indirectly. The absolute claim here is factually incorrect and weakens the evaluation.

inResponse.head: Unsupported 'highly effective' judgement
inResponse.quote: Overall the strategies were highly effective, mostly because of price skimming, and Northline should keep cutting prices to reach its 12 per cent target
inResponse.why: The conclusion calls the strategies 'highly effective' but no evidence in the response confirms that Northline reached or approached its 12 per cent target. An evaluation requires the outcome to be measured against the objective. Without that, the judgement is asserted rather than proven.

profiles.summary: This is a focused, well-argued response that holds one judgement from start to finish and supports it with specific, quantified evidence from Northline Sportswear. The main gap is business terminology: the strategies are described in plain English rather than named and framed using course concepts, which limits the mark in criteria 1, 3 and 4.

inResponse.head: Name the key concepts
inResponse.quote: I would judge Northline Sportswear's marketing as mostly successful, measured against the specific goal the business set itself: in 2023 it wanted a bigger slice of the market made up of 13 to 17 year olds, moving from 8 per cent of that market to 12
inResponse.why: The response describes the objective but does not use the term {{market share|the percentage of total sales in a market held by one business|0}} or {{target market|the specific group of customers a business directs its marketing toward|0}}. Naming these concepts signals to the marker that your argument is grounded in course knowledge.

inResponse.head: Name the promotional strategy
inResponse.quote: The switch away from print toward short videos did what it was meant to do
inResponse.why: Describing a 'switch away from print toward short videos' is accurate but earns less than naming it as a shift in the {{promotion|communication strategies used to inform and persuade target customers|0}} mix, specifically toward {{digital marketing|use of internet-based channels to reach target audiences|0}}. Using the term connects the evidence to course content.

inResponse.head: Add a limitation to complete the evaluation
inResponse.quote: The money was buying the right audience, and buying it cheaply
inResponse.why: A strong evaluation acknowledges what the strategy did not do as well as what it did. Website visits are not the same as {{market share|the percentage of total sales in a market held by one business|0}}: the response does not state whether rising visits converted to purchases. Noting this gap would complete the evaluative judgement.

inResponse.head: Name the strategy type
inResponse.quote: The app for members did a different job
inResponse.why: The loyalty app is a form of {{relationship marketing|strategies aimed at building long-term customer loyalty and repeat purchases|0}}. Naming it tells the marker you are applying a course concept rather than just describing a feature of the business.

inResponse.head: Name the pricing strategy
inResponse.quote: Where Northline went wrong was price
inResponse.why: A broad price reduction across the whole range is likely a {{penetration pricing|setting a low price to gain market share quickly|0}} or discount pricing strategy. Naming the type of pricing decision shows the marker that you are evaluating a specific course concept rather than a general business choice.

inResponse.head: Use 'brand positioning' here
inResponse.quote: A brand trying to look desirable to teenagers through its videos was telling them at the same time that it was a discount label
inResponse.why: This sentence makes a strong point about {{brand positioning|the way a business wants customers to perceive its brand relative to competitors|0}}, but it does not use the term. Adding it would earn marks under criterion 3 without changing your argument.

inResponse.head: Reinforce the evaluative judgement with course language
inResponse.quote: So the goal was nearly reached, with share ending at 11 per cent, but the discounting gave away margin and will probably cost it some of what it gained
inResponse.why: The conclusion is accurate and honest, but 'will probably cost it some of what it gained' is an assertion without a mechanism. Linking this to {{brand image|the perception customers hold of a brand, built over time through all marketing activities|0}} or the long-term sustainability of market share would complete the evaluation and close the response with course-level reasoning.

inResponse.head: Missing overall judgement
inResponse.quote: Northline Sportswear's marketing objective for 2023 was to lift its share of the 13 to 17 year old market from 8 to 12 per cent, and its strategies are best judged against that number
inResponse.why: The sentence names the {{marketing objective|a specific, measurable goal that guides a business's marketing decisions|0}} and sets a clear benchmark, which is strong. However, it does not signal whether the strategies were, on balance, effective or not, so a marker cannot yet see a thesis to follow. An introduction that also states the verdict earns the response a higher mark from the first line.

inResponse.head: Evidence not closed against the objective
inResponse.quote: The business reported a cost per view of 4 cents against 19 cents for its print campaigns, and site visits from the target age group rose by a third within six months, so the strategy reached the intended buyers more cheaply
inResponse.why: The sentence uses the data well to show efficiency, but it does not say whether this movement in site visits brought Northline closer to the 12 per cent share target. Tying the evidence back to the objective number gives the evaluation its full mark.

inResponse.head: Incomplete sentence, no explanation of harm
inResponse.quote: Northline cut prices across its range in the same year, and
inResponse.why: The sentence stops mid-clause, so the paragraph does not explain how the price cut undermined the {{marketing objective|a specific, measurable goal that guides a business's marketing decisions|0}}. A marker cannot award evaluation marks for an unfinished argument. The paragraph needs to say what the price cut did and why that made the 12 per cent share target harder to reach.

inResponse.head: Missing key marketing terms
inResponse.quote: I would judge Northline Sportswear's marketing as mostly successful, measured against the specific goal the business set itself: in 2023 it wanted a bigger slice of the market made up of 13 to 17 year olds, moving from 8 per cent of that market to 12
inResponse.why: The paragraph identifies a measurable objective and a {{target market|the specific group of consumers a business directs its marketing toward|0}}, but never uses those terms. In HSC Business Studies, naming the concept alongside the evidence is what lifts a response into the upper bands, because it shows you understand the category, not just the example.

inResponse.head: Strategy not named as a promotional strategy
inResponse.quote: The switch away from print toward short videos did what it was meant to do
inResponse.why: Calling it 'the switch away from print toward short videos' describes the action but does not identify it as a {{promotional strategy|a method a business uses to communicate with its target market and stimulate demand|0}} or as {{digital marketing|using online and social media platforms to reach consumers|0}}. Naming the strategy type earns marks under the terminology criterion.

inResponse.head: Evaluation stops at efficiency, not effectiveness
inResponse.quote: The money was buying the right audience, and buying it cheaply
inResponse.why: The sentence shows the strategy was cost-efficient but does not connect this to movement toward the market share objective. In an evaluate question, effectiveness means showing impact on the stated goal, not just value for money.

inResponse.head: Strategy not named as relationship marketing or CRM
inResponse.quote: The app for members did a different job
inResponse.why: The membership app is a form of {{relationship marketing|strategies designed to build long-term loyalty and repeat purchasing rather than one-off sales|0}}, often called {{customer relationship management (CRM)|systems and practices that manage a business's interactions with existing customers to increase retention|0}}. Naming it earns marks under the terminology criterion and signals you understand which part of the marketing mix it belongs to.

inResponse.head: Retention cost claim is asserted without support
inResponse.quote: Getting a teenager to try the brand once does not move the share figure for long; getting them to keep returning does, and keeping a customer costs less than winning a new one
inResponse.why: The claim that retention is cheaper than acquisition is a well-known principle, but the response states it as if it is self-evident rather than connecting it to Northline's actual figures or naming it as a business concept. Without evidence or a term, it reads as personal opinion rather than analysis.

inResponse.head: Pricing strategy not named
inResponse.quote: It made everything cheaper in the same year, and the average amount spent per sale dropped by 11 per cent
inResponse.why: The decision to lower all prices is a {{pricing strategy|the method a business uses to set the price of its products, which affects both revenue and brand perception|0}}, likely a form of {{penetration pricing|setting a low price to attract new customers and grow market share|0}} or broad discounting. Naming the strategy type connects your example to the course concept and earns marks under the terminology criterion.

inResponse.head: Use 'brand positioning' instead of 'a discount label'
inResponse.quote: A brand trying to look desirable to teenagers through its videos was telling them at the same time that it was a discount label
inResponse.why: The idea you are describing is {{brand positioning|the way a business places its brand in consumers' minds relative to competitors, often based on price, quality or lifestyle|0}}. Using that term here would turn an informal observation into a business studies argument.

upheld.claim: Says there is no conclusion, although the student's final one-sentence paragraph is clearly meant as one. It also asks the student to refer back to objectives 'named in the introduction' when none were named.
Unexplained shorthand 'P1' in a heading shown to the student.
Two whole-response observations appear under 'In your response' with empty quotation marks, while 'Across your response' is empty.
(Hidden, not shown.) The stored rubric bands contradict the scores: a score of 0 is labelled band '1-2', and one criterion has band null.
The promotion observation writes the analytical link for the student. It also presupposes an 'awareness objective' that the response never states.

Several visible items supply the content the student should have thought of: the objectives, the purpose of the delivery threshold, the rationale for the product range. These are suggestions rather than full sentences, but they come close to answering the question for the student.

Says the student must name 'at least two' objectives, which neither the question nor the marking points require ('States the marketing objectives being judged against'). Also overstates the effect of doing so.
A whole-response observation appears under 'In your response' with an empty quotation, while 'Across your response' is empty. In total, ten deficit-only items are shown for a six-paragraph response.
The mark of 17 is about 5 marks too high for a response that has an evaluative frame but no case-study evidence and an objective with no target.
Comparative failure: the middle response (17) scores above the strong response (16). The two make the same argument, but only the strong one supports it with quantified evidence.

The conclusion observation says the conclusion repeats an earlier summary. No such summary exists: the conclusion is the first place the outcome is stated and the pricing limit is weighed. The suggestion to judge short-term versus long-term threat partly duplicates what the student already wrote.
The band language in the summary contradicts the mark: a 17/20 is described as Band 5 and as held out of Band 6.
Hidden rubric: the stored bands do not fit the scores, e.g. application scored 5/6 but given band 3-4. This is not shown to the student.
The strongest response in the corpus scores 16, below the evidence-free middle response (17). Strong must not be outranked by a weaker equivalent.
The main stated reason for the deduction penalises accurate plain-English expression of concepts the student clearly uses, which is a wording penalty.

The pricing observation says the student does not connect the price cut to brand positioning, and calls the paragraph observation rather than analysis. The student explicitly links the price cut to the premium image.
The conclusion advice tells the student to tie the judgement to the benchmark, which they already do. It also overstates what P4 established in order to argue against a reasonable hedge.
The advice to replace the specific case detail 'loyalty app' with a generic label would weaken case-study application, and the observation promises marks for doing it.

The reach-to-share observation (a valid point) says the gap limits the 'sustained' criterion, but the stored rubric gives that criterion full marks. Its empty quote also leaves unclear which paragraph it means.
The summary never tells the student that the quantified, objective-linked evidence is the response's defining strength. It also uses band language ('upper band') rather than explaining the mark.
The feedback switches to third person, addressing the reader as 'the student'. Hidden rubric bands also do not fit the scores (4/7 in band '7-8').

The response's accurate general knowledge gets no credit in the mark: the hidden rubric scores knowledge 0/5. The visible notes say this content cannot be rewarded at all, rather than telling the student it earns knowledge credit but no application credit.

The conclusion note says the conclusion repeats the opening 'word-for-word in effect' and is headed 'restates thesis'. This is false, and it contradicts the marker's own earlier note that there is no thesis.

The marker relabels the student's general point about price cuts as 'market penetration pricing'. Penetration pricing means setting a low entry price; cutting the prices of an existing premium range is discounting or a price reduction.
One note switches to the third person ('The student'), while every other note addresses the student as 'you'. It also mentions 'the chosen business' when no business was chosen.

6/20 undervalues the response. It ties the purely descriptive er15-descriptive (6) and sits below the fact-listing er15-case-heavy (8), even though its knowledge, terminology and argument are much stronger than either.
The response's defining strength, accurate and purposeful syllabus knowledge, is scored 1/5 in the stored rubric. The 1/5 score also conflicts with its own band of '3-4'.

The summary criticises the response for brevity ('short plan'), against the instruction to mark what is there and inconsistently with how equally short responses were treated. The response is continuous prose with a connected argument, not a plan.

The 'No tie-back' note says the pricing paragraph never judges the pricing strategy, but the student says discounting undermined the premium position at Northline. The note also refers to 'Northline's stated marketing objectives', which the marker elsewhere says were never stated.
The marker says the pricing topic sentence 'restates' a principle, but nothing earlier states it. It is a valid topic sentence that the next sentence applies to Northline, if thinly.

The pricing observation says the student cannot evaluate a strategy without naming it with a course label, and it says no pricing strategy was named although the student identified it in plain words. The label it supplies, 'competitive pricing', is also speculative, because the response gives no comparison with rivals.

The feedback writes the analytical inference for the student instead of prompting them to draw it. The inference is also overstated given the student's own data: average sale value fell 11 per cent, and a member/non-member gap does not by itself show the app caused the difference.

Three of the ten observations are about attaching course labels, and two of them present the label as what turns description into argument. This pulls attention away from the response's real deficit, which is that it makes no judgement.

The pricing observation ignores the most evaluable fact in that paragraph, the student's own 11 per cent fall in average sale value. That fact is where the tension between discounting and the objective could have been pointed out.
In the stored rubric (not displayed), band labels do not match scores, and criterion maxima differ from other profiles of the same question.

1/20 is the same mark as er15-weak, although this stub names the business, states a market-share objective and a strategy that fits it, none of which er15-weak does. The stored rubric gives knowledge 0 and application 0 despite this content, and labels those zero scores band '1-2'.
The summary says no judgement appears anywhere. In fact the student begins an (unsupported) effectiveness judgement, which the marker itself acknowledges in a later observation.

Four of the seven 'In your response' entries have empty quotes, so they display as empty quotations. They describe absences across the whole response and belong under 'Across your response', which is empty. 'No overall judgement stated' also repeats the point already made in 'Objective needs evaluative framing'.

The summary says the most important fix is the mislabelled term. The larger problems are the reasoning errors (absolute claims about sales and profit, dismissing the 11 per cent fall, no reported outcome). A student who only relabelled the strategy would keep most of the faults.
The marker overstates the effect of a single error on the mark. It says the wrong label alone forfeits all marks for the strategy, and that removing 'always' is required for any marks.

The visible feedback never credits the response's real attempt to weigh effectiveness: an explicit ranking of the three strategies, a single line of argument held to the conclusion, and a recommendation. These are evaluative moves, even though the reasoning behind them is wrong.
Stored (not displayed): the rubric bands do not match the scores. The knowledge criterion scores 1 of 6 but is labelled band "3-4".

Stored (not displayed): the ladder model sentences contradict the marker's own critique. They assert that the pricing strategy "drove meaningful progress" and that social media was "the strongest contributor", and the response contains no evidence for either claim.

The marker says the conclusion's warning about future losses has no mechanism. The previous paragraph supplies one in plain words: discounting signals a cheap brand and undermines the desirability the videos built, and it costs margin. For the same content in the original strong response, the marker said paragraph four had already established it.

The feedback says outright that identical content earns fewer marks in plain English. It extends the penalty to the knowledge and coherence criteria, not just terminology, even though the same summary says the response holds one judgement throughout.

The visible observations never acknowledge the response's strongest analytical move: explaining why retention, not one-off trial, is what moves the share objective. They also do not acknowledge the verdict in the opening sentence. Six of the seven observations are vocabulary requests.

The pricing observation suggests that evaluating a business decision is weaker than evaluating a course concept, but the question asks for an evaluation of the business's strategies. Labelling an across-the-range price cut as "likely" penetration pricing is also loose, because penetration pricing usually means a low price at market entry.

Stored (not displayed): the rubric contradicts the visible explanation. Terminology, which the summary calls "the main gap", scores 4/5, while knowledge scores lowest at 3/5. The bands also do not match the scores (3/5 labelled "7-8").

15/20 is too high for a response with no overall judgement, no outcome measured against the objective and an unfinished counter-argument. It is only one mark below the complete strong response (16) and equal to the complete reworded strong response (15), so finishing the weighing and conclusion is worth about one mark.

In the stored paragraph scoring, all 20 marks go to the four paragraphs the student wrote, with no conclusion or judgement slot. The missing conclusion therefore cost no marks, and the loyalty paragraph scores higher here than the identical paragraph in the complete response. This contradicts the summary's claim that the missing conclusion is a main source of lost marks, and it explains the inflated total.

The stored rubric data (not shown) is internally inconsistent. Criterion maximums differ from the other profiles (8/6/3/3 instead of 5 each), and the band labels do not match the scores. The stored ladder also contains raw glossary-token markup.
